newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Share analysts welcome BHP's bitter pill.
newsitem.headline: Share analysts welcome BHP's bitter pill.

text.p: Australian share analysts on Friday welcomed The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd's decision to further clean up its balance sheet but said asset sales must follow.
BHP earlier on Friday reported a 61 percent dive in net annual profit to A$410 million for the year ended May 31, after booking huge abnormal losses of almost A$1 billion.
The losses stemmed mainly from writing down the value of underperforming assets in BHP's copper, minerals and petroleum divisions. The steel division took restructuring charges.
"They have certainly wiped the slate clean...," one Melbourne-based analyst told Reuters.
"They are being very aggressive to generate profit growth and I think it will come through," he added.
But the analyst, who declined to be named, said investors now expected BHP to get some assets off its books altogether.
The Melbourne analyst said he expected the group to announce asset sales to the tune of about A$1.5 billion for the current year ending May 31, 1998.
"The bulk of that A$1.5 billion would be coming out of the minerals division, not so much copper," he said.
The analyst also speculated that BHP could sell some of its recently-acquired North America operations, including the Pinto Valley, Superior and Robinson mines.
Market talk has also centred on the Tintaya mine in Peru.
BHP acquired the Tintaya and North America operations in January 1996 when it bought Magma Copper Co for US$2.4 billion -- a price criticised by analysts sometime later as too high.
A Sydney-based analyst, who also declined to be identified, said asset sales would complete BHP's restructuring process.
"It's not all over," the analyst said.
"The evidence that the restructuring is serious will be that the underperforming assets get sold and they chop out the A$500 million in costs they talked about in steel," he added.
Another Melbourne-based analyst welcomed the write-downs but said he did not see the restructuring exercise being finalised anytime soon.
"Restructuring takes years," he said.
The analysts said they were revising their profit forecasts for BHP in 1997/98, based not only lower depreciation charges on the slimmed-down assets, but also on improved operations.
In the May quarter, the copper and steel business both showed improvements in underlying profit. The copper business was helped by a rally in the world copper price.
But analysts warned that further falls in the copper price would continue to put pressure on BHP's share price, which is still trading at a price-earnings multiple of over 20 times.
BHP shares dipped immediately after the earnings announcement, but then bounced back. At 0450 GMT, BHP shares were trading at A$19.14, up eight cents on Thursday's close.
-- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1421
